intro: `Insomnia` is an API client for designing, debugging and testing APIs. You can send REST, GraphQL and gRPC requests, inspect the responses and keep your requests organised in collections.
It suits developers who want a clean desktop app to try an endpoint, compare environments and share requests with a team.

capabilities.title: Many protocols
capabilities.text: Work with REST, GraphQL and gRPC from the same app.

capabilities.title: Collections
capabilities.text: Group related requests into folders so a whole API is easy to browse.

capabilities.title: Environments
capabilities.text: Keep base URLs and tokens in variables and switch between development and production in a click.

capabilities.title: Response viewer
capabilities.text: See status, headers, timing and a formatted body side by side.

capabilities.title: Import and export
capabilities.text: Bring in requests from other tools or an OpenAPI file instead of retyping them.

helps: Insomnia helps you check how an API really behaves before you write client code. Send a request, read the response and adjust until it works.
Because requests are saved, you can repeat the same checks later or hand them to a teammate.
why: Developers like Insomnia for its uncluttered interface and quick start. It does the common jobs well without a long setup.
Support for GraphQL and gRPC next to plain REST makes it handy for teams that mix API styles.

workflows.title: Explore a new API
workflows.text: Import its OpenAPI file, then try each endpoint from the generated requests.

workflows.title: Switch environments
workflows.text: Point the same requests at local, staging or production by changing the active environment.

workflows.title: Debug a failing call
workflows.text: Inspect headers, status codes and timing to see where a request goes wrong.

workflows.title: Share with a team
workflows.text: Export or sync a collection so everyone tests the same requests.

beyond.purpose: Store variables such as base URLs and tokens
Reuse a value from one response in the next request
Turn a request into a snippet you can paste into your project
Extend the app with community add-ons
Run tests and checks from the command line and CI

tips: Create separate environments for local, staging and production on day one.
Name requests clearly so a collection reads like documentation.
Keep secrets in environment variables, not inside request bodies.
Use folders that mirror your API's structure.
Save a request as soon as it works so you can rerun it later.
audience: Insomnia suits backend and frontend developers, QA engineers and anyone who needs to test APIs by hand.
It is a good choice when you want a focused API client without a lot of extra features to learn.

intro: `Postman` is an API platform for building, testing, documenting and monitoring APIs. It began as a simple tool for sending requests and has grown into a full workspace for API work.
Teams use it to keep requests, tests and documentation in one place so everyone works from the same source.

capabilities.title: Request builder
capabilities.text: Create and send requests, then inspect the response body, headers and timing.

capabilities.title: Collections
capabilities.text: Organise requests into folders and share them with your team.

capabilities.title: Environments
capabilities.text: Use variables to switch between local, staging and production setups.

capabilities.title: Automated tests
capabilities.text: Write JavaScript tests that check status codes and response data.

capabilities.title: Mock servers
capabilities.text: Simulate an API before the real backend is ready.

capabilities.title: Documentation
capabilities.text: Generate readable API docs from your collections.

helps: Postman lets you try an API quickly and then turn those manual checks into repeatable tests.
It also gives frontend and backend teams a shared reference, so they agree on how an endpoint should behave.
why: Postman covers the whole API workflow in one app, from the first test request to documentation and monitoring.
Its large user base means plenty of tutorials, templates and public collections to learn from.

workflows.title: Test an endpoint
workflows.text: Build a request, send it and compare the response with what you expect.

workflows.title: Automate checks
workflows.text: Add tests to a collection and run it with the collection runner.

workflows.title: Collaborate
workflows.text: Share a workspace so teammates use the same collections and environments.

workflows.title: Mock before building
workflows.text: Create a mock server so the frontend can start while the backend is in progress.

workflows.title: Monitor an API
workflows.text: Schedule collection runs to see whether an API stays healthy.

beyond.purpose: Run code before a request, for example to create a timestamp
Check status codes and response data after a request
Run many requests in order
Run collections from the command line and CI
Return example responses from a fake API
Run collections on a schedule

tips: Use environments instead of hard-coding URLs and tokens.
Add at least a status-code test to every important request.
Group requests in folders that match your API's structure.
Save example responses so teammates see what to expect.
Keep secrets in variables and avoid sharing them in public workspaces.
audience: Postman is useful for developers, testers and API designers, and for any team that builds or consumes APIs.
It works for a quick one-off request as well as for a full automated test suite.

intro: `jq` is a lightweight command-line processor for JSON. It reads JSON, applies a filter you write and prints the result, much like `sed` or `grep` do for plain text.
Because most APIs and many config files use JSON, jq has become a standard way to inspect and reshape that data right in the terminal.

capabilities.title: Filtering
capabilities.text: Pick out exactly the fields you need from a large JSON document.

capabilities.title: Transforming
capabilities.text: Reshape data, rename keys and build new objects.

capabilities.title: Pipelines
capabilities.text: Chain filters with the pipe symbol, just like shell commands.

capabilities.title: Built-in functions
capabilities.text: Use functions such as `map`, `select`, `sort_by` and `length`.

capabilities.title: Pretty printing
capabilities.text: Turn minified JSON into readable, coloured output.

helps: jq lets you answer questions about JSON without writing a script. Need the names of all users older than 30? One short filter does it.
It also fits naturally into shell scripts, where its output can feed other commands.
why: jq is small and fast, and it has no dependencies, so it is easy to install on servers and in CI images.
Its filter language is compact. Once you learn a handful of patterns, you can handle most everyday JSON tasks.

commands.note: Keep items that match a condition
Collect one field from each item
Print a raw string without quotes

workflows.title: Inspect an API response
workflows.text: Pipe the output of `curl` into jq to read only the fields you care about.

workflows.title: Extract values for scripts
workflows.text: Use `-r` to get plain text that a shell script can use.

workflows.title: Clean config files
workflows.text: Reformat or edit JSON configuration in a repeatable way.

workflows.title: Search logs
workflows.text: Filter JSON log lines to find the entries that matter.

beyond.purpose: Output raw text instead of JSON strings
Print compact one-line JSON
Pass a shell variable into a filter
Read all inputs into a single array
Keep only values that match a test
List the keys of an object

tips: Start with `jq .` to see the structure before writing a filter.
Build filters one step at a time and check the output at each step.
Put filters in single quotes so the shell leaves them alone.
Use `-r` when you need plain text for scripts.
Keep a few favourite one-liners in your notes.
audience: jq is useful for developers, DevOps engineers, data analysts and anyone who works with JSON from APIs, logs or config files.
If you already live in the terminal, it quickly becomes a tool you reach for every day.

intro: `Neovim` is an extensible, keyboard-driven text editor that grew out of Vim. It keeps Vim's fast modal editing and adds a modern codebase, built-in language server support and Lua scripting.
It runs in the terminal, so it feels the same on your laptop and on a remote server.

capabilities.title: Modal editing
capabilities.text: Separate modes for typing and for commands make editing fast once you learn them.

capabilities.title: Lua configuration
capabilities.text: Write your setup in Lua instead of older Vim script.

capabilities.title: Built-in LSP client
capabilities.text: Get diagnostics, go-to-definition and completion from language servers.

capabilities.title: Tree-sitter
capabilities.text: Fast, accurate syntax highlighting based on code structure.

capabilities.title: Built-in terminal
capabilities.text: Open a shell inside the editor.

capabilities.title: Plugin ecosystem
capabilities.text: Add file explorers, fuzzy finders and many other tools.

helps: Neovim lets you edit code without leaving the keyboard. Moving, selecting and changing text all become short key sequences.
You can shape it into a light text editor or a full coding environment, depending on the plugins you add.
why: People choose Neovim for speed, low resource use and the freedom to configure everything.
It works the same over SSH, which makes it a favourite for working on servers.

commands.note: Enter insert mode and start typing

workflows.title: Quick edits on a server
workflows.text: Open a config file over SSH, change it and save, with no graphical tools.

workflows.title: Full coding setup
workflows.text: Add language server and syntax plugins to get completion and diagnostics.

workflows.title: Refactoring with macros
workflows.text: Record a series of edits once and replay it many times.

workflows.title: Multi-file work
workflows.text: Use splits and tabs to view several files at once.

beyond.purpose: Your main configuration file
Install and update plugins
Diagnose problems with your setup
Record and replay a sequence of edits
View several files in one window
Read the built-in documentation

tips: Run `:Tutor` first. It is a short, hands-on lesson inside the editor.
Start with a small configuration and add plugins one at a time.
Learn a few motions such as `w`, `b` and `e` before anything advanced.
Use `:help` when you are stuck, since the docs are thorough.
Keep your configuration in version control.
audience: Neovim is a good fit for developers who enjoy keyboard-driven workflows, and for anyone who edits files over SSH.
It rewards time spent learning, so it suits people who want to build an editor around how they work.

intro: `Visual Studio Code` is a free, lightweight code editor from Microsoft that runs on Windows, macOS and Linux. It supports many languages out of the box and grows through extensions.
It sits between a simple text editor and a full IDE: quick to open, yet capable enough for large projects.

capabilities.title: IntelliSense
capabilities.text: Smart completion, parameter hints and quick information as you type.

capabilities.title: Extensions
capabilities.text: Add languages, themes, linters and tools from the marketplace.

capabilities.title: Integrated terminal
capabilities.text: Run commands without leaving the editor.

capabilities.title: Built-in Git
capabilities.text: See changes, stage files and commit from the sidebar.

capabilities.title: Debugging
capabilities.text: Set breakpoints and step through code in the editor.

capabilities.title: Remote development
capabilities.text: Work over SSH, inside containers or in WSL as if the code were local.

helps: VS Code gives you one place to write, run, debug and version your code, so you switch between fewer tools.
You can start with the defaults and add only the extensions your projects need.
why: It is free, quick to start and works almost everywhere, which is why so many developers and teams adopt it.
A huge extension library means that nearly every language and framework has good support.

commands.note: Jump to a file by name

workflows.title: Web development
workflows.text: Edit code, run a dev server in the terminal and debug in the browser from one window.

workflows.title: Git workflow
workflows.text: Review diffs, stage changes and commit without leaving the editor.

workflows.title: Remote work
workflows.text: Open a folder on a server or in a container and edit it directly.

workflows.title: Team consistency
workflows.text: Share workspace settings and recommended extensions with your team.

beyond.purpose: Keep settings and extensions the same across machines
Save settings that apply to one project
Run build and test commands from the editor
Insert reusable pieces of code
Develop inside a container with a ready environment
Switch between setups for different kinds of work

tips: Learn the Command Palette first. Almost every feature is one search away.
Shortcuts above are for Windows and Linux. On macOS use Cmd instead of Ctrl.
Install only the extensions you need to keep the editor fast.
Turn on format on save so your code stays tidy.
Use workspace settings for project-specific rules.
audience: VS Code suits beginners and professionals alike, across web, backend, data and scripting work.
If you want one editor for many languages, it is an easy place to start.
